title: Design a Large-Scale Web Crawler
prompt: Design a web crawler that fetches and stores billions of web pages for a search index. It must be polite to hosts, avoid re-crawling duplicate content, handle the scale and messiness of the open web, and keep making progress despite failures.
blurb: The URL frontier, politeness, dedup with bloom filters, DNS, and petabyte-scale storage.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (fetch, parse, extract links, store, recrawl) from non-functional (scale, politeness, freshness, robustness, extensibility).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about scale/pages, freshness/recrawl needs, content types, respect for robots.txt, dedup expectations.

rubric.label: Estimations
rubric.description: Estimates pages, fetch rate, bandwidth, storage (raw + parsed), frontier size, dedup structure size.

rubric.label: URL frontier
rubric.description: Prioritized + politeness-partitioned queue design; front/back queues, per-host queues, priority.

rubric.label: Politeness & robots
rubric.description: Per-host rate limiting, crawl-delay/robots.txt, avoiding hammering a host across distributed workers.

rubric.label: Deduplication
rubric.description: URL dedup (seen set, bloom filter) and content dedup (checksums/simhash for near-duplicates).

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Frontier → fetchers → parser → link extractor → dedup → storage, with DNS + robots caches.

rubric.label: DNS & fetching
rubric.description: DNS resolution caching (a real bottleneck), connection reuse, timeouts, retries, trap avoidance.

rubric.label: Storage
rubric.description: Raw page store (blob), parsed content, link graph; petabyte scale, compression.

rubric.label: Scaling & robustness
rubric.description: Distributed fetchers, sharding the frontier, crawler traps, spider-trap and infinite-space handling, checkpointing.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Crawl rate, error rates by host, frontier depth, freshness, politeness violations.

functional_requirements: Fetch web pages starting from seed URLs
Parse pages and extract new links to enqueue
Store raw + parsed content for the index
Deduplicate URLs and detect duplicate/near-duplicate content
nonfunctional_requirements: Polite — never overload a single host
Robust to malformed pages, traps, slow/dead hosts
Extensible to new content types and parsers
Makes steady progress; resumable after failures
clarifying_questions: Target corpus size and crawl rate (pages/day)?
How fresh must content be — recrawl cadence?
Which content types — HTML only, or also PDFs/images?
Must we strictly honor robots.txt and crawl-delay?
Do we need near-duplicate detection or just exact-URL dedup?
qualifying_questions: Is politeness per-host or per-IP (multiple hosts share an IP)?

estimations.traffic: Crawl 10B pages/month ≈ ~4K pages/s sustained; must burst higher to absorb slow hosts
estimations.storage: Raw ~1PB/month (compressed ~200-300TB); parsed text + link graph additional; store in blob + columnar
estimations.dedup: Seen-URL set for 100B+ URLs — a bloom filter at ~10 bits/URL ≈ ~125GB, vs TBs for exact sets

data_model: frontier: prioritized queues, partitioned into per-host back-queues for politeness
seen_urls: bloom filter (fast negative) + backing KV of URL hashes (confirm)
content_index(url_hash, content_checksum, simhash, last_crawled, http_status, etag)
pages_raw: blob store keyed by url_hash (compressed HTML)
api_design: Internal next_url(fetcher_id) → politeness-respecting URL to fetch
Internal store(url, raw_bytes, parsed, links) → persistence + dedup
Admin: submit seed set, adjust priority/recrawl policy
reference.high_level_design: Seeds enter the URL frontier, which is a two-level structure: front queues encode priority (importance/freshness) and back queues enforce politeness by pinning each host to a single back-queue so only one fetcher hits a host at a time, honoring its crawl-delay. Fetcher workers pull URLs, resolve DNS (via a cache — DNS is a real bottleneck), check the cached robots.txt, download the page, and hand raw bytes to the parser. The parser extracts links; each candidate URL is normalized and checked against a bloom filter (and a backing seen-store on positives) before being enqueued, avoiding re-crawls. Content is checksummed/simhashed to drop exact and near-duplicates before storage. Raw pages go to blob storage; parsed text and the link graph go to indexable stores. A scheduler decides recrawl timing per page based on change frequency.

deep_dives.probe: Design the frontier so it's both prioritized and polite. Ten thousand fetchers, and you must never send two concurrent requests to the same host. How do the front and back queues achieve that?
Politeness is per-host, but fetchers are distributed. How do you guarantee only one worker hits example.com at a time and respects its crawl-delay across the whole fleet?

You've seen tens of billions of URLs. An exact set is too big for memory. How does a bloom filter help, what's the false-positive cost, and how do you also catch near-duplicate *content* (not just URLs)?
DNS resolution is often the crawler's hidden bottleneck. Why, and how do you cache/parallelize it? How do you handle spider traps and infinite URL spaces?
You cache robots.txt and DNS with TTLs. When a hugely popular host's robots/DNS cache entry expires and thousands of queued URLs need it, how do you avoid a stampede of simultaneous lookups?

Crawled pages land in a content store. How do you feed the downstream search-index pipeline off it — change data capture with something like Debezium, or emit events from the crawler directly? How do you handle recrawl updates vs first-crawls?

followup_bank.question: How do you make the frontier both prioritized and polite at once — what's the role of front queues vs per-host back queues?
Across distributed fetchers, how do you guarantee only one worker hits a host at a time and honors crawl-delay?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions bloom filter or dedup or seen
followup_bank.question: What's the false-positive rate you target for the seen-URL bloom filter, what does a false positive cost you, and how do you also detect near-duplicate content?
Why is DNS a crawler bottleneck, and how do you cache and parallelize resolution without overwhelming resolvers?
For DNS/robots caches, what eviction/TTL policy, and how do you avoid a stampede when a popular host's entry expires?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or store or index
followup_bank.question: How do you propagate crawled/updated pages to the search index — CDC/Debezium vs crawler-emitted events — and how do you distinguish recrawl updates from new pages?
How do you detect and escape spider traps and infinite URL spaces (calendars, faceted params)?

scaling: Shard the frontier and dedup structures by URL/host hash across nodes
Distribute fetchers by host partition so politeness stays local to a shard
Aggressive DNS + robots caching to cut per-fetch overhead
Compress raw pages; tier storage (hot recent vs cold archive)
Checkpoint frontier and seen-state so a crawl resumes after failures
bottlenecks: Politeness limiting effective per-host throughput (slow hosts stall queues)
Dedup structure memory at tens of billions of URLs
Storage write bandwidth at petabyte scale
Spider traps / infinite spaces wasting crawl budget
tradeoffs: Bloom filter (compact, small false-positive rate → occasional skipped URL) vs exact set (accurate, huge)
Politeness (respectful, slower per host) vs raw throughput
Exact content dedup (checksum) vs near-dup detection (simhash, fuzzier but catches templated pages)
Freshness (frequent recrawl, more load) vs cost
alternative_solutions: Priority frontier driven by PageRank-like importance instead of pure BFS
Distributed dedup via sharded exact key-value store instead of bloom filter (when accuracy matters)
Sitemap/feed-driven discovery to reduce blind link-following
Focused/topical crawler that scores relevance before fetching
observability: Crawl throughput (pages/s) and success vs error rates by host/status
Frontier depth and per-host queue backlog
Freshness (age distribution of crawled content) and politeness-violation alerts
security: Honor robots.txt and nofollow; identify with a proper User-Agent
Sandbox/parse untrusted content safely (avoid parser exploits, zip bombs)
Bound resource use per host to avoid being (or being seen as) a DoS
Filter malicious/malware URLs from the index
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer centers on the URL frontier as a two-level queue: front queues for priority/freshness and per-host back queues that pin each host to one fetcher so politeness (crawl-delay) holds across a distributed fleet. It dedups URLs with a bloom filter plus a backing seen-store (reasoning about false positives) and dedups content with checksums/simhash for near-duplicates. It calls out DNS resolution as a real hidden bottleneck and caches DNS + robots.txt, handles spider traps and infinite spaces, and stores raw pages compressed in blob storage with parsed text and a link graph for the index. It proactively raises politeness-limited throughput, dedup memory, and storage bandwidth as bottlenecks, covers recrawl/freshness scheduling and checkpointing for resumability, and addresses CDC vs crawler-emitted events to feed the index.

interviewer_notes: The URL frontier is the heart of this question — if the candidate treats it as a plain queue, interrupt and force the priority-plus-politeness two-level design. Politeness across distributed fetchers is the key senior probe: push until they explain how only one worker hits a host at a time and honors crawl-delay. Make them reason about the seen-URL bloom filter's false-positive tradeoff and, separately, near-duplicate content detection — many miss the content-dedup half. DNS as a hidden bottleneck is a good differentiator; raise it if they don't. If they place a content store, fire the CDC/Debezium probe; if they add DNS/robots caches, fire the eviction/stampede probe. Reserve the end for spider traps, freshness/recrawl, and resumability.
